lesson.title: Nonresponse Bias: When the Silent Ones Differ
lesson.summary: Nonresponse bias arises when individuals who were properly selected for a sample fail to respond, and those who do respond differ systematically from those who don't, skewing the results even though selection itself was random.
lesson.body:
Nonresponse bias is easy to confuse with undercoverage, but the two happen at different stages of a study, and the distinction matters. Undercoverage means someone never had a chance to be selected in the first place, because the sampling frame left them out. Nonresponse bias means someone was selected, they were on the list, they received the survey, they were called, but they chose not to answer, and the people who do answer turn out to differ systematically from the people who don't. The sample selection can be flawless, a true simple random sample of every eligible person, and nonresponse bias can still creep in entirely at the response stage.

Response rates below 100 percent are the rule rather than the exception in real surveys, and a low response rate is not automatically disqualifying on its own. The danger arises specifically when nonresponse is not random, when the kind of person who ignores a survey differs in relevant ways from the kind of person who fills it out. Busy working parents might be less likely to complete a lengthy phone survey than retirees with more free time; people who feel strongly dissatisfied with a company might refuse a customer satisfaction survey out of frustration, while satisfied customers happily respond, or the reverse could hold depending on the topic. Whenever the reason for not responding is tangled up with the answer the question would have produced, the responses that do come in no longer represent the full sample that was selected.

Consider a hypothetical example. A school district randomly selects 800 parents, a genuine simple random sample from the full roster of enrolled students' families, to survey about satisfaction with a new online homework portal. Only 240 parents complete the survey, a 30 percent response rate. Suppose parents who found the new portal frustrating or confusing were also the ones too busy or too irritated to spend ten minutes on a follow-up survey about it, while parents who found the portal smooth and easy had a more pleasant recent experience and felt more inclined to respond. The 240 responses would then skew toward satisfaction even though the original 800 names were selected with no bias whatsoever, because the silence of the frustrated parents was not random silence.

The remedy for nonresponse bias is different from the remedy for undercoverage. Since the selection process was already sound, the fix focuses on raising response rates through reminder calls, multiple contact attempts, alternative response formats, or incentives, and on checking whether respondents differ from non-respondents on any measurable trait, comparing grade levels or geographic areas of responding versus non-responding families, for instance, to gauge how large a distortion might be present. None of this changes who was originally sampled; it targets the gap between who was asked and who actually answered.

Nonresponse bias is a reminder that bias, the general concept running through this entire set of sampling and design ideas, can enter a study at more than one point: in how the population is defined, in how the frame is built, in how individuals are selected from the frame, and, as nonresponse bias shows, in whether the selected individuals actually respond once asked. A study can get every earlier step right, a representative frame, a genuinely random selection, and still end up with a misleading picture if the people who stay silent are not a random cross-section of the people who were asked to speak.
